lead.t: A pituitary disorder is any condition that impairs the normal structure or function of the pituitary gland, leading to excess or deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.

snip.t: A pituitary disorder is any condition that impairs the normal structure or function of the pituitary gland, leading to excess or deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.
*After reading this note you will be able to recognise, investigate and outline the acute and definitive management of common pituitary disorders seen in Kenyan clinical rotations.
Pituitary disorders include hyperpituitarism (e.g., adenomas causing hormone excess or mass effects) and hypopituitarism (deficiency of pituitary hormones).

qs.q: Which pituitary disorder is characterized by excessive secretion of ACTH, leading to hypercortisolism, central obesity, and a moon face?
qs.e: Cushing's Disease is caused by excessive secretion of ACTH from a pituitary adenoma, which overstimulates the adrenal glands to produce excess cortisol. Hyperprolactinemia involves excess prolactin leading to galactorrhea rather than hypercortisolism.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and a bitemporal visual field defect – what is the most likely diagnosis and next investigation? — Prolactinoma; obtain serum prolactin and visual field testing.

A postpartum woman develops fatigue, hypotension and hyponatraemia; cortisol is 2 µg/dL. What is the immediate management? — Treat adrenal crisis with IV hydrocortisone before any other hormone replacement.

A patient with known pituitary macroadenoma develops sudden severe headache and ophthalmoplegia. What complication should you suspect and how do you confirm it? — Pituitary apoplexy; urgent MRI or CT if MRI unavailable.

How does secondary Cushing disease differ from ectopic ACTH production on laboratory testing? — Both have high cortisol, but ACTH is normal/high in both; however, ectopic ACTH often shows lack of diurnal variation and higher cortisol after high‑dose dexamethasone suppression.

Why is cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine for prolactinoma in resource‑limited settings? — Cabergoline has higher efficacy, fewer side effects, and requires less frequent dosing, improving adherence.

A child with short stature has low IGF‑1 and low GH on stimulation testing; MRI shows a pituitary stalk lesion. What is the most likely cause in this region? — Infiltrative infection such as TB; treat TB and consider GH replacement after infection control.

What are the key components of long‑term follow‑up for a patient after trans‑sphenoidal surgery for a GH‑secreting adenoma? — Annual IGF‑1, MRI at 6‑12 months, monitor glucose and blood pressure, assess for hypopituitarism.

During a routine exam a patient on levothyroxine for secondary hypothyroidism reports new fatigue and weight loss; labs show low TSH and low free T4. What is the likely explanation? — Under‑replacement of thyroxine; adjust dose after confirming adequate cortisol coverage.
ai.title: Pituitary Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pituitary disorders are conditions that impair the gland’s structure or hormone output, causing excess or deficiency. In low‑resource East African settings, common causes include adenomas, infiltrative infections and postpartum necrosis. Recognising clinical patterns guides targeted investigations and urgent management.

b: Hyperpituitarism: hormone excess with mass effect.
Hypopituitarism: deficiency of ≥1 anterior pituitary hormone.
sections.p: Any disease that alters pituitary anatomy or hormone secretion, producing either hormone excess (hyperpituitarism) or deficiency (hypopituitarism). Diagnosis rests on clinical syndrome plus targeted hormone assays and imaging when available.

b: Stage I: isolated hormone loss, stable.
Stage II: multiple hormone deficits, no crisis.
Stage III: acute endocrine emergency (e.g., adrenal crisis).
sections.p: Severity is staged by hormone deficit number and acute versus chronic presentation. Acute adrenal crisis or severe hyponatraemia denotes high‑risk disease.

b: Hyperpituitarism: pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma, GH‑secreting, ACTH‑secreting).
Hypopituitarism: postpartum pituitary necrosis (Sheehan), infiltrative infections (TB, HIV‑related opportunistic infections), pituitary apoplexy, radiation, traumatic head injury.
sections.p: Identify the most common aetiologies in East Africa and rank them by likelihood for each presentation.

b: Prolactinoma: galactorrhoea, menstrual disturbance, infertility, visual field loss.
GH excess: acromegaly (adult) or gigantism (child).
ACTH excess: Cushingoid features, hypertension, hyperglycaemia.
Hypopituitarism: fatigue, loss of libido, amenorrhoea, cold intolerance, hypotension, hyponatraemia.
sections.p: Symptoms reflect the hormone(s) involved and any mass effect on surrounding structures.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; provide alternatives when resources are limited.

t.b: Is prolactin excess present? Elevated >20 µg/L in men, >25 µg/L in women suggests prolactinoma.
Is GH excess likely? Low‑normal IGF‑1 rules out acromegaly; high IGF‑1 supports diagnosis.
Is adrenal insufficiency present? <3 µg/dL indicates need for urgent glucocorticoid replacement.
Is secondary hypothyroidism present? Low free T4 with normal/low TSH confirms pituitary origin.
Is a structural lesion present? Detects adenoma, apoplexy, infiltrative disease. If MRI unavailable, use CT head as a fallback.
Is there a mass effect on optic chiasm? Bitemporal hemianopia suggests macroadenoma.

b: Adrenal crisis: hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia.
Pituitary apoplexy: sudden severe headache, ophthalmoplegia, altered consciousness.
Severe hypercortisolism: uncontrolled hypertension, infection risk.
Uncontrolled hyperprolactinaemia causing visual loss.
sections.p: Identify life‑threatening sequelae that require immediate action.

b: Adenoma causing excess hormone: surgery (trans‑sphenoidal) when available; otherwise dopamine agonist (cabergoline) for prolactinoma, somatostatin analogue for GH excess.
Hypopituitarism: replace glucocorticoids first, then thyroxine, sex steroids, GH (children only).
Sheehan syndrome: lifelong hormone replacement; monitor for adrenal crisis.
Infection‑related hypopituitarism: treat TB/HIV opportunistic infection, then replace hormones.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, replace deficient hormones, and address mass effects.

b: Annual hormone panel (cortisol, TSH, free T4, LH/FSH, IGF‑1).
Repeat imaging at 6‑12 months after surgery or when symptoms change.
Patient education on stress‑dose steroids and sick‑day rules.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring prevents recurrence and detects treatment complications.

b: Primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low T4) vs secondary (low/normal TSH).
Ectopic ACTH production (small‑cell lung cancer) vs Cushing disease.
Polycystic ovary syndrome causing hyperprolactinaemia‑like menstrual changes.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic pituitary hormone abnormalities.

b: Stress‑induced cortisol rise may mask adrenal insufficiency; obtain early morning sample.
Macroprolactin can cause falsely high prolactin; consider polyethylene glycol precipitation if available.
Low IGF‑1 in malnutrition may mimic GH deficiency.
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that are common in low‑resource labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache with visual loss (possible apoplexy).
Hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia suggesting adrenal crisis.
Rapid progression of visual field defect.
